opus-5.5.text:
So, it's a really interesting question, because the capabilities keep changing faster than we can properly evaluate them. When I look at systems like GPT-4o, Claude 3, Gemini, they're already performing at a level that, in many domains, is better than the average human. If you take a random person off the street and give them a set of exams across law, medicine, programming, poetry, these systems will outperform most people on most of those tasks. That, to me, already looks like a form of general intelligence. Not superintelligence yet, but definitely more general than anything we had just a few years ago.

What concerns me is that we don't actually know the full extent of what they can do. Capabilities are discovered after deployment. People find new prompts, new ways of chaining the models together, giving them tools, memory, internet access, and suddenly the system can do things the developers never tested for. So any assessment we make is really a lower bound. We're measuring what we've thought to ask, not what the system is truly capable of.

And then there's the trajectory. Each new generation is noticeably more capable than the previous one, and the gap between "impressive chatbot" and "system that can do meaningful independent work in science, engineering, hacking" is shrinking. Some of the people building these systems openly predict human-level AGI within a few years, and given what I see, I don't think that's unreasonable.

The part that worries me most is that capability is growing exponentially, while our ability to control, explain, predict, or verify these systems is basically not growing at all. We can't fully explain why they give a particular answer. We can't guarantee they won't behave badly in some novel situation. So when people ask me how good they are, my honest answer is: good enough that we should be very concerned, and getting better much faster than our safety tools are.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is: nobody really knows, including the people who built them. And that's the part that should worry us.

Capability-wise, these systems are already surprisingly good. Look at GPT-4o or Claude 3, they pass the bar exam, they do well on medical licensing tests, they write code, they explain jokes. A few years ago I would have said those are things we don't know how to do, and now they're commodity. Groq is a slightly different animal, that's really about speed of inference, but speed matters too, because it changes what you can deploy and how fast these things act in the world.

But here's what I actually care about. We cannot predict what a model will be able to do before we train it. The developers finish training, and then they spend months discovering capabilities they didn't know were in there. That's not engineering in the traditional sense. That's more like archaeology. You dig and you find things. And if you can't predict the capabilities, you certainly can't predict the failure modes, and you can't guarantee safety.

So when people ask me, are these systems dangerous today, I say probably not in the sense of taking over the world. They still make mistakes, they hallucinate, they're not agentic enough yet. But every generation is a step. GPT-3 to GPT-4 was a big jump. The step from GPT-4 to whatever comes next will be bigger, because there's more compute, more data, more money. And the safety work is not keeping up with the capability work. It's not even close. We're building something we don't understand, we can't verify, we can't explain, and we are scaling it as fast as physically possible.

So my assessment is: impressive, unpredictable, and getting more so. If you're asking whether I'm comfortable, no. I'm not.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re impressive, but their capabilities are very uneven. You can ask a difficult programming question and get a useful answer, then ask something seemingly trivial and watch the same system fail. That makes it difficult to describe their intelligence with a single number or benchmark.

I would also distinguish the model from the infrastructure running it. Groq is primarily about inference hardware and speed, whereas GPT-4o, Claude, and Gemini are models or model families. Speed matters, but it isn’t the same thing as intelligence.

From my perspective, the important question is reliability. A system producing an impressive answer doesn’t establish that we can trust it across unfamiliar situations. And as we give these systems more autonomy, the gap between what they can do and what we can reliably predict about their behavior becomes increasingly important.

r001.rationale: The response describes capabilities as uneven and distinguishes Groq’s inference hardware from the other systems; it does not judge all four as roughly equal overall.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim these systems outperform an average person across all possible tasks. It emphasizes uneven performance and reliability concerns.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re incredibly impressive, but also very uneven. You can ask a system a difficult question and get what looks like an expert answer, and then it fails on something a child would find obvious. So it’s hard to describe their capabilities with a single number or say they’re at a particular human level.

I would also separate capability from reliability. Demonstrating that a model can solve a problem is different from knowing that it will solve it correctly when you need it to. And neither tells you whether you can control its behavior as it becomes more capable.

For me, that’s the central issue. We’re getting better at building systems that produce impressive results. That doesn’t automatically mean we’re getting better at understanding them or guaranteeing that they’ll do what we intended.
